Discussion Permanent vision loss (PVL) from GCA has been reported in 8% to 19% of patients, with bilateral blindness occurring in 2.7% to 5.1% of patients. However, definitions of PVL amongst studies vary and are often not well defined with many not reporting visual acuity and few commenting on visual field loss. compares results from our study with eight other studies reporting on patients with PVL from temporal arteritis, listed in order of publication year. In their retrospective study of 245 patients, Aiello et al. reported 34 (14%) with permanent vision loss: 11 patients ‘complete blindness one eye’; 1 patient ‘complete blindness both eye’; 15 patients ‘partial deficit one eye’; and 7 patients ‘partial deficit both eyes’. Thirty-two of their 34 patients presented with PVL prior to diagnosis and treatment. Acuity values are only listed for 10 patients with PVL who had visual changes during treatment, acuities ranging from 20/20 to NLP, with “altitudinal visual field loss’ noted in two patients. Salvarani et al. noted 41 of their 136 GCA patients (30%) had visual manifestations and 25 of their 26 PVL patients presented with ‘partial or total vision loss.” Singh et al. reported vision changes in 47 of 204 cases (23%) with PVL in 18 (9%) and 4.4% complete vision loss, but did not supply details on acuity nor visual field testing. Causes of PVL in 53 (16%) of a cohort of 334 patients (all temporal artery biopsy positive) described by Liozon et al. included AION, CRAO, PION, but they as well had no data on visual acuities. Yates et al. analyzed 34 patients (7.9% of a cohort of 433 GCA patients) with ‘complete loss of vision’, but noted a formal ophthalmology assessment was not carried out routinely so could not define further. Hočevar et al. noted visual symptoms in 56 (19%), and PVL (defined as acuity < 20/200 in either eye) occurring in 22 (7.6%) of their 295-patient-cohort, but did not have data on lesser degrees of acuity loss nor visual field changes. Dumont et al. restricted their definition of PVL as acuity < 1/20, occurring in 42 (10%) of their 409 GCA patients, only 79 with positive temporal artery biopsies. Amsler et noted visual acuity for the 26 eyes of their 21 patients: decimal acuity ≥0.5 (20/40 or better) in 11; <0.5 and ≥0.3 in 1; <0.3 and ≥0.1 in 3; and < 0.05 (<20/400) in 9 eyes, and unknown in two eyes. Statistically significant predictors of vision loss in our study Age and jaw claudication The most frequent reported risk factors for PVL amongst studies are increasing age and jaw claudication, which we found to be risk factors in our study as well. We found the adjusted (multivariate) odds ratio (OR) for a one-year increase in age at diagnosis was 1.05, indicating that we can expect a 5% increase in the odds of having PVL per year of increased age. Most other studies report similar 1.06 to 1.08 OR for PVL with increasing age. , Jaw claudication was present in 65.5% of our patients with PVL versus 46.8% without vision loss, OR 2.29, p = .04. Lack of polymyalgia rheumatica and headache Polymyalgia rheumatica and headaches were present in 20.0% and 56.4% of our PVL patients respectively compared to 46.0% and 84.7% of patients without PVL. We found the odds of a patient without PMR developing PVL to be three times higher (OR 3.07) compared to patients with PMR. Similarly, patients without headache were 4.25 times more likely to develop PVL, compared to those with headaches. Significant lower clinical or laboratory activity among GCA patients with ischemic complications was first observed over 2 decades ago by Cid el al. Since this finding, the majority of researchers also report PVL to be associated with lower level of acute phase reactants, CRP and more variably erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR). , , , , Theoretic postulations on increased risk of blindness for patients with lower CRP at presentation include propensity for inflammation in smaller vessels or possibly a diagnostic delay. A strong inflammatory response could decrease the risk of ischemic lesions through the local angiogenic function of proinflammatory cytokines, principally interleukin 6 (IL-6). A lower tissue circulating level of IL-6 was demonstrated in GCA patients with ischemic complications compared to those without them. Other authors did not find PVL associated with lower acute phase reactant. , , In their review of 14,574 patients (3,728 TAB positive), Therkildsen et al. found the risk of ocular manifestations did not differ between patients with low or high levels of CRP or ESR. This research does not allow us to determine if one route is superior in preventing permanent vision loss, nor determine effect of dose, initiation nor duration on risk for PVL. Studies have not found intravenous steroids better than oral steroids in preventing further vision loss, , , , however when signs of ocular ischemia are present, intravenous delivery can ensure high levels quickly. Limitations of our study include the retrospective nature of the data set with missing data information. Onset of some symptoms including headache, jaw claudication and more vague vision changes such as “floaters,” ‘blurred vision,” and visual field defects may not be accurately noted by patients, and therefore, data may underestimate the duration of these preceding symptoms. Headache and neck pain were only recorded when the patient and physician described it as such. Severe ear or base of skull pain was considered headache; there may be a higher under-reported percentage of patients with neck pain. In a multivariate analysis, the effect of each variable is reported independent of its associations with the other variables (the p values for each predictor are calculated as if all the other predictors were constant). Another limitation is the lack of genetic analyses, as studies suggest not only a genetic susceptibility of developing GCA, but also possibly phenotypes at risk of severe ischemic complications. Conclusions For patients with suspected GCA, concern for possible ocular ischemic events should be particularly high with increasing age, jaw claudication, ocular symptoms and increased platelets. Importantly, lack of rheumatic symptoms of headache and polymyalgia and lower levels of C-reactive protein may be a more ominous indication for risk of ocular involvement. As reported by others, we found ocular involvement often resulted in severe vision loss with little chance of recovery. We found a third (34.5%) of our GCA patients had visual symptoms and a fifth (21.7%) suffered PVL. For patients with PVL, 38% had bilateral clinical involvement and for 80% of these patients the vision loss was severe to acuity of CF or less and/or dense visual field defect of −20 decibels of greater.
